lastAfter:
The Dohkar’s hands stayed raised, the ceremonial sash across his chest catching the filtered light like a second accusation. The youth’s wrist was still in my grip, her wrist shifting once against the callus at the base of my thumb. Around us the circle of First Favored had drawn so tight that the Weave-Script on their arms brushed mine when they shifted.

“Speak,” the Dohkar said. His voice carried the weight of the rite’s broken **binding**. “Tell us what you did to turn her words.”

I opened my mouth and the words came out thin, scraped raw by the eyes on me. “I did nothing. The wish was hers. I only stepped forward when the misalignment hit. That is what any Sacrificiant would do.”

A murmur ran through the crowd like wind through dry grass. Someone near the back muttered that the name the youth had spoken belonged to Julian, and that alone was proof enough of **spell**craft. The youth tried to pull free, a fine scale at the edge of her cuff lifting under the pad of my index finger. I loosened my hold but did not let go entirely.

“She twisted the sacrifice herself,” I said, louder now so the words would reach the outer ring. “She offered discipline and named my father. That was her choice, not mine. The Dohkar felt the same misalignment I did. Ask him.”

The Dohkar’s thumb dragged once along the seam of his sash. His own Weave-Script had settled into a slow, warning pulse of amber along his throat. “I felt it. I also felt the **contract** that led straight to you. You carry his name in your blood. The child reached for it like a beacon.”

My heel caught and held against a raised root beneath the mat. I could feel the crowd waiting for me to deny it, to claim distance I did not have. The tarot deck was still in my other hand, its frayed corner edge catching the ridge of an old scar. I had not meant to bring it here. I had not meant for any of this to surface under the mated-pair trees.

Striking before she was pretty, the kind of face that made people hesitate before they looked away, I tilted my head slightly, listening. A wide, full mouth shaped for either cruelty or tenderness framed by soft cheekbones and an expressive brow turned toward the Dohkar, the dark brown waves of my hair loose over my shoulders catching the light. “I did not call him,” I said. The words tasted like iron. “I have not spoken his name in years. If the child reached for him, she reached on her own.”

The youth’s gaze flicked to mine and away again, shame and something sharper moving across her face. She opened her mouth as if to speak, then closed it when the Dohkar stepped closer. The ceremonial band across my own mouth had been torn free minutes ago; I could still feel the ghost of the cloth against my lips.

The Dohkar studied me for a long moment. “Then prove it,” he said. “Stand aside and let the rite finish without you. If the wish was clean, it will hold. If it was not, the misalignment will name its source.”

The crowd waited. The youth waited. My fingers tightened once around the deck before I forced them still.

Present.

As the weight of the moment pressed down on me, I felt the urgency to act. I had to decide whether to petition the Alignment Circle to re-bind the energies at play, to seek clarity amidst the chaos. The choice loomed before me, a path that could either sever the ties of blood or reinforce them in ways I couldn't yet fathom.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If Fate truly listened, I would ask it to make the Dohkar see that the child acted alone. No. I would ask it to bring Julian here so he could speak the truth I cannot make them hear.

ringTail: The youth knelt on the crimson spiralgrass , her aqua skin catching the filtered light beneath the mated-pair trees. She lifted her voice and twisted the practiced words into a blade aimed straight at the Dohkar. "I offer the discipline to finish my studies," the youth declared, "but let it bring Lirael the father who left her instead." The Dohkar's head snapped up. Two dozen First Favored surged forward on bare feet, their Weave-Script flaring violent reds across arms and throats as the crowd closed the circle tighter around the rite. The misalignment struck like a physical blow. My ribs locked. I tore the gossamer band from my mouth and stepped between the youth and the Dohkar before the next breath could land. Protocol shattered under my feet. The youth's eyes widened but she did not retreat. A guest at the edge of the clearing shouted without warning, "That name belongs to the man Julian once shielded in the Long Thread villages. Everyone here knows the connection now." The Dohkar's hands rose in demand. "Explain the corruption of the sacrifice or forfeit your own place." The crowd's silence pressed against my skin like heated stone. I crossed the remaining distance to the youth, seized her wrist, and pulled her upright so the rite could not continue without me standing inside it. My shoulder burned where the ceremonial sash dragged. The guest kept speaking, his voice carrying the weight of Julian's reputation like a second accusation. "She used the child to draw him back into the open." The youth's Weave-Script stuttered with panic. I refused to release her wrist. "The rite belongs to her alone," I said, voice steady even as the Dohkar advanced. "Any claim on my past ends here." The crowd shifted again, bodies pressing closer, forcing My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I didn't remember bringing it. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.
